title: System Script Proxy Execution: SyncAppvPublishingServer
summary: SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs is a Microsoft-signed Visual Basic script that ships with the App-V client, which is the Microsoft Application Virtualization component that presents virtualised Win32 applications to users as if they were installed locally. The script lives in the System32 directory and is normally invoked through wscript.exe, the Windows script host, and it accepts a delimited argument string in which a caller can place a command for the host to run. Adversaries abuse that argument contract by embedding a PowerShell command in the argument, so the resulting process tree shows a trusted signed script host handing execution to the interpreter rather than a user launching it directly. Detection depends on process and script telemetry: command lines that pair wscript.exe with SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs and inline command text, unusual parent-child relationships such as wscript.exe spawning powershell.exe or a console host, PowerShell script block logging capturing the decoded payload, and script host events showing execution from System32 with attacker-supplied arguments. Legitimate App-V activity originates from the App-V client service during a publishing refresh, carries no inline command text, and repeats on a predictable schedule, which is the main discriminator a defender can use.

beginner.definition: SyncAppvPublishingServer is a small script file that comes with Windows. It supports App-V, which stands for Application Virtualization, a feature that lets programs run as if they were installed on your computer. The script is signed by Microsoft, so many tools trust it by name alone.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools often trust files that Microsoft has signed. When an attacker runs a command through a trusted script, many alarms stay quiet. This approach is called living off the land, which means using the tools already present on the computer. You must watch what a trusted script starts, not only the name of the script.
howItWorks: Windows installs the App-V client, which stands for Application Virtualization and runs programs without a normal installation.
The file SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs sits in the System32 folder and is usually started by wscript.exe, the Windows script host.
The script accepts one long argument. A semicolon splits that argument, and the second part can hold a command to run.
An attacker calls the script and places a PowerShell command in that second part, so the script passes it to the system.
The result is a signed script that starts PowerShell, which looks far less suspicious than a user calling PowerShell directly.
Defenders must read the command line and the parent process, because the script name on its own looks completely normal.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital where only approved staff can open the medicine room. A cleaner carries a badge that opens many doors, because cleaners must move supplies everywhere in the building. An attacker borrows that cleaner badge and walks into the medicine room. The door log shows a valid badge, so nobody is alarmed at first. Guards who check only badges miss the problem. Guards who also ask why a cleaner is in the medicine room at three in the morning notice it straight away.
takeaways: A signed Windows script can be used to run an attacker's command.
Watch the parent process and the command line, not just the program name.
Normal App-V activity does not carry command text inside its arguments.

objectives: Explain what the SyncAppvPublishingServer script does in a normal Windows installation.
Describe how an attacker can use this signed script to run PowerShell commands.
Identify which process creation fields reveal this abuse on a host.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the System Script Proxy Execution parent technique.
List two signs that separate normal App-V activity from attacker activity.
